los.text: Identify the parts of the adult heart, both externally and internally, and explain their functional significance
los.html:
• Outside: apex (LV, 5th left intercostal space)
    • base (posterior surface, mainly left atrium)
    • sternocostal surface mainly right ventricle
    • diaphragmatic surface both ventricles
    • coronary (AV) and interventricular sulci carry the vessels.
ChamberKey featuresFunction
Right atrium
  • Smooth sinus venarum vs rough pectinate muscles, divided by the crista terminalis
  • Openings of SVC, IVC, coronary sinus
  • Fossa ovalis
  • SA node
Receives systemic venous blood
Right ventricleTrabeculae carneae, 3 papillary muscles, moderator band (carries right bundle branch), smooth infundibulum to pulmonary valveLow-pressure pump to lungs
Left atriumMostly smooth; 4 pulmonary veins; left auricle (clot forms here in AF)Receives oxygenated blood
Left ventricleThickest wall (~3× RV), 2 papillary muscles, aortic vestibuleHigh-pressure systemic pump
SeptaInteratrial (fossa ovalis = old foramen ovale); interventricular (muscular, plus a thin membranous upper part where VSDs are common).
Valves
  • AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) tethered by chordae and papillary muscles
  • Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) with 3 cusps
  • Coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses.
Fibrous skeletonRings anchor the valves and insulate atria from ventricles electrically, except through the AV bundle.

los.text: Locate the atrio-ventricular, pulmonary and aortic valves on an intact heart, demonstrate their surface markings in the living and how they relate to clinical and radiological examinations and describe their role in the prevention of regurgitation of blood, and know where they can best be auscultated
los.html:
ValveLies behindBest heard
PulmonaryLeft 3rd costal cartilage (the highest valve)2nd left intercostal space beside the sternum
AorticSternum at the 3rd intercostal space2nd right intercostal space beside the sternum
MitralLeft 4th costal cartilageApex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line)
TricuspidSternum at the 4th intercostal spaceLower left sternal edge (4th–5th space)
Why the differenceSound carries downstream with the blood, so each valve is heard where its outflow comes nearest the chest wall ("All People Enjoy Time Magazine": aortic, pulmonary, Erb's point, tricuspid, mitral).
Preventing backflow
  • AV valves close at the start of systole (S1)
  • Papillary muscles pull on chordae so the cusps don't evert.
  • Semilunar cusps fill and meet at the end of systole (S2).

los.text: Label the parts of the conducting system of the heart on a diagram
los.html:
1. SA nodein the right atrial wall where the SVC meets the top of the crista terminalis.
2. Atrial pathwaysInternodal tracts; Bachmann's bundle to the left atrium.
3. AV nodein the interatrial septum near the coronary sinus opening (triangle of Koch).
4. AV bundle (of His)Pierces the fibrous skeleton into the membranous septum.
5. Bundle branchesRight (via the moderator band) and left (anterior and posterior fascicles).
6. Purkinje fibresUnder the endocardium of both ventricles.
  • Blood supply: SA node from the RCA in ~60%
    • AV node from the RCA in ~80–90%, which is why inferior MI causes heart block.

los.text: Describe the anatomical course of the spread of excitation through the chambers of the heart
los.html:
1. SA node fires(60–100/min)The pacemaker because it is the fastest.
2Atria depolarise cell to cell and contract (P wave).
3. AV node delay(~0.1 s)Lets the ventricles fill; the only electrical route through the fibrous skeleton (PR interval).
4. His bundle and bundle branchesDown the septum (septum depolarises left to right first).
5. Purkinje fibresApex first, then up the walls, so the ventricles squeeze from apex to base towards the outflow tracts (QRS).
  • Backup rates: AV junction 40–60/min, ventricles 20–40/min.

los.text: Locate surface anatomy landmarks with respect to the heart (and great vessels), being aware of how they relate to clinical and radiological examinations including the placement of ECG electrodes
los.html:
Heart outline
  • Upper border 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage
  • Right border 3rd–6th right cartilage just beside the sternum (right atrium)
  • Inferior border 6th right cartilage to the apex (mainly RV)
  • Left border apex up to the 2nd left space (LV).
Great vesselsSVC behind the right 1st–3rd cartilages; aortic arch behind the manubrium; pulmonary trunk at the 2nd left space.
ECG leadPosition
V14th intercostal space, right sternal edge
V24th intercostal space, left sternal edge
V3Midway between V2 and V4
V45th intercostal space, midclavicular line
V5Anterior axillary line, level with V4
V6Mid-axillary line, level with V4
  • Limb leads: right arm, left arm, left leg (right leg = neutral).

los.text: Describe the effects of sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation on the heart
los.html:
EffectSympatheticParasympathetic
SourceT1–4/5 via cardiac nerves from the sympathetic trunkVagus cardiac branches
Receptorβ1M2
Heart rate↑↓
Contractility↑ (atria and ventricles)Little (atria only)
AV conduction↑↓
  • At rest: vagal tone dominates (intrinsic SA rate ~100/min, resting rate 60–80).

los.text: Locate the cardiac plexus and recall that it contains both sympathetic and parasympathetic (from the vagus nerve) fibres
los.html:
LocationSuperficial part below the aortic arch; deep part in front of the tracheal bifurcation (behind the arch).
ContentsSympathetic cardiac nerves (cervical and upper thoracic ganglia) + parasympathetic cardiac branches of the vagus (including from the recurrent laryngeal nerves) + visceral afferents.
DistributionAlong the coronary arteries to the SA and AV nodes, atria and ventricles.

los.text: Explain the mechanism of 'referred pain' as it relates to myocardial ischaemia
los.html:
MechanismPain afferents from the heart run back with sympathetic fibres to spinal segments T1–T4(5).
ConvergenceThe same segments carry skin sensation from the chest wall and medial arm (T1–T2, intercostobrachial nerve), so the brain reads the pain as coming from there.
Typical patternCentral chest, down the left arm (medial side), into the neck and jaw, sometimes epigastrium.
Silent MIDiabetics and the elderly (autonomic neuropathy) may feel little pain.

los.text: Identify the right and left vagus nerves, right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves and sympathetic chains
los.html:
Right vagus
  • Crosses in front of the right subclavian artery
  • → right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery
  • → vagus runs behind the right lung root onto the oesophagus (posterior vagal trunk).
Left vagus
  • Between left common carotid and subclavian
  • → crosses the aortic arch
  • → left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum
  • → behind the left lung root (anterior vagal trunk).
Recurrent laryngeal nervesUp the tracheo-oesophageal grooves to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
  • Left RLN is longer and in the chest
  • So hoarseness can come from lung cancer
  • Aortic aneurysm
  • Mediastinal nodes or a huge left atrium.
Sympathetic chainsBeside the vertebral bodies (over the rib heads in the thorax); cervical ganglia (superior, middle, inferior/stellate) give cardiac nerves.

los.text: Identify right, inferior and left heart borders and their constituent parts on a chest radiograph
los.html:
BorderFormed by
RightSVC (upper), right atrium (lower)
LeftAortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left atrial appendage, left ventricle
InferiorRight ventricle (mostly), LV apex
Silhouette signRight heart border lost → right middle lobe problem; left border lost → lingula; hemidiaphragm lost → lower lobe.
Left atrial enlargementDouble right heart border, splayed carina.

los.text: Recognise chest radiographs that are taken in two ways: posteroanterior (PA) and anteroposterior (AP)
los.html:
ViewBeamEffect
PA (standard)Back to front; detector against the front of the chest; standingHeart close to the detector → little magnification; scapulae rotated out of the lung fields
APFront to back; bedside or supine, unwell patientsHeart further from the detector → magnified; scapulae over the lungs; often poorer inspiration
  • Rule: you can't reliably judge heart size on an AP film.

los.text: Describe how the cardiothoracic ratio is determined on a PA chest radiograph
los.html:
Cardiothoracic ratioWidest horizontal heart diameter ÷ widest internal thoracic diameter (inner rib edges, usually at the diaphragm), on a PA film.
Heart widthMidline to right border + midline to left border.
Normal< 0.5; above 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.
Only valid on PAAP films magnify the heart.
